analysis.one_liner: Caps credit card interest rates at 16% and most credit card fees at $15.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in a House Financial Services subcommittee from February 2012 until the Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have written a national 16% ceiling into law for credit card interest rates, counting annual and membership fees toward that ceiling so issuers could not charge them on top. It also would have capped late fees, overdraft fees, and over-the-limit fees at $15, and made it an unfair practice for a card issuer to raise a rate on any account that was below 16% during a window around the bill's introduction. Today there is no federal limit on credit card interest rates, and late fees can run far higher than $15.
analysis.who_benefits: People who carry credit card balances, especially those paying rates above 16%, which is most borrowers who revolve debt. Anyone hit with late, overdraft, or over-the-limit fees would have paid no more than $15 per fee. The bill also counted annual and membership fees toward the 16% cap, so a card charging a $95 annual fee could not also charge 16% interest without breaching the ceiling.

how_it_helps.text: Caps the annual percentage rate on any credit card balance at 16%, and folds annual or membership fees into that calculation so issuers cannot collect them outside the cap [S2][S3].
Caps late fees, overdraft fees, insufficient-funds fees, and over-the-limit fees at $15 per fee [S2][S3].

Treats any rate increase on an account that was below 16% as of February 8, 2012 as an unfair or deceptive practice during the period between that date and 60 days after enactment, discouraging issuers from raising rates while the bill moved [S2][S3].

Allows the Federal Reserve to raise the ceiling only if it finds severe economic conditions justify it, with a presumption that increases are not in the public interest, a notice to Congress, a mandatory House Financial Services hearing, and a 90-day window in which Congress could block the increase [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Credit card issuers, which are banks and card companies. They would lose interest income on balances currently priced above 16% and fee income above $15 per fee. The industry's standard argument is that some of that cost gets shifted to borrowers: customers with the weakest credit could be denied cards or offered lower credit limits, because issuers price risk through rates and fees.

drawbacks.text: A hard 16% ceiling flattens risk-based pricing. Borrowers with poor credit, who currently pay higher rates to compensate for default risk, could lose access to credit cards entirely rather than get cheaper ones [S3].

Capping fees at $15 does not reduce how much a late borrower owes in total; issuers could respond by raising the interest rate on balances (up to the 16% cap) or tightening credit standards, so the savings for high-risk borrowers may be smaller than the fee numbers suggest [S3].

The retroactive provision treating rate increases between February 8, 2012 and enactment as unfair or deceptive reaches back to conduct that was legal when it happened, which is an unusual legal posture even for supporters of rate caps [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the majority of cardholders who carry balances at rates well above 16%, the benefit is direct and large: the average credit card rate is far above 16%, so the cap would have cut interest costs substantially, and the $15 fee cap would have eliminated fees that commonly run $25-$40. The main cost falls on a concentrated industry, with a secondary risk that the least creditworthy borrowers lose access to cards rather than gain cheaper credit. That access concern is real but it is the same objection raised against every usury cap, and the bill's design (a ceiling with a narrow Federal Reserve escape valve) addresses it only partially.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and then to its Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit subcommittee, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Tierney introduced the bill on February 17, 2012, joined by 14 Democratic cosponsors and no Republicans [S1][S3][S4].
The House referred it to the Financial Services Committee and also to the Rules Committee on the day of introduction [S1][S5].
Six days later it was referred to the Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit subcommittee, and that is the last action on record [S5].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote is recorded before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit card issuers and banks, which continued charging interest rates above 16% and late and over-limit fees above $15 for the rest of the Congress and after. No borrower benefited from the bill's death.

for.name: Rep. John Tierney
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cap credit card APRs at 16% and most fees at $15.

for.name: 14 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; included members such as Louise Slaughter, Peter DeFazio, George Miller, James McGovern, Jesse Jackson Jr., Dennis Kucinich, Marcy Kaptur, Jan Schakowsky, Mazie Hirono, and Raul Grijalva.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee leadership
against.role: Controlled the committee calendar in the 112th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it in subcommittee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 15 supporters were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored; the bill then died in a committee controlled by the House Republican majority without any recorded vote.

industries.industry: Credit card issuers (banks and card companies)
industries.note: The bill would cut interest income on every balance priced above 16% and cap late, overdraft, and over-limit fees at $15, and would fold annual fees into the rate cap. Issuers' revenue in this market comes directly from charges to cardholders, so the industry's gain runs against consumers' cost. The bill never advanced, so issuers kept the current pricing structure.
